steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "By site" section of the encyclopedia article on algorithmic radicalization, with a subsection each on Facebook, YouTube and TikTok describing how their recommendation algorithms relate to radical content.

### YouTube

### TikTok

steps.text:
### Facebook
- algorithm recommends content that makes user want to interact

- interests list on "Your ad Preferences" page; Pew Research: 74% of users didn't know it existed until directed there in the study
- relatively common for Facebook to assign political labels
- recent years: AI changes feed content + recommendations
- The Facebook Files: AI prioritizes user engagement over everything; controlling AI systems difficult
- August 2019 internal memo, leaked 2021: [quote: "the mechanics of our platforms are not neutral"]
  - max profits -> optimization for engagement necessary
  - algorithms found hate, misinformation, politics instrumental for app activity
  - [quote: "The more incendiary the material..."]
- 2018 study: [quote: false rumors spread faster and wider; 70% more likely retweeted on Twitter; first 1,500 people six times faster; stronger for political news]
### YouTube
- since 2005; more than 2.5 billion monthly users
- discovery systems use personal activity (watched, favorites, likes) -> recommended content
- algorithm accounts for roughly 70% of recommended videos, drives what people watch
- 2022 Mozilla Foundation study: users have little power to keep unsolicited videos out of recommendations (hate speech, livestreams, etc.)

  - Al-Qaeda and similar extremist groups: recruitment videos, engaging international media outlets
- study in American Behavioral Scientist Journal: [quote: "whether it is possible to identify a set of attributes..."]
  - result: extremism recommendations factor in radical keywords in video titles

### TikTok
- videos recommended to 'For You Page' (FYP); every user's page different
- FYP linked to more explicit and radical videos over time based on previous interactions
- since inception scrutinized for misinformation, hate speech -> generate more interactions
- 2022: head of US Security statement: [quote: 81,518,334 videos removed globally April – June] -> cut back hate speech, harassment, misinformation
- radicalization cases
  - early 2023: Austrian authorities thwarted plot against LGBTQ+ pride parade; two teenagers and a 20-year-old inspired by jihadist content on TikTok
    - youngest 14, exposed to Islamist influencers glorifying jihad -> more engagement -> planning attack
  - 2024: teenagers arrested in Vienna planning terrorist attack at Taylor Swift concert; some radicalized online, TikTok one of the platforms spreading extremist content

steps.text:
### Facebook

The algorithm of Facebook is focused on recommending content that makes the user want to interact. It ranks content by giving priority to popular posts by friends, viral content, and sometimes divisive content. Every feed is personalized to the specific interests of the user, and this can sometimes lead users towards an echo chamber of troublesome content. Users can find the list of interests the algorithm uses by going to the "Your ad Preferences" page. A Pew Research study found that 74% of Facebook users did not know the list existed until the study directed them to that page. It is also fairly common for Facebook to assign political labels to its users. In recent years Facebook has started to use artificial intelligence to change the content that users see in their feed and what gets recommended to them. A document called The Facebook Files revealed that the AI system puts user engagement above everything else. The Facebook Files also showed that the AI systems have been difficult to control.

In an internal memo from August 2019 that was leaked in 2021, Facebook admitted that "the mechanics of our platforms are not neutral", and concluded that optimization for engagement is necessary to reach maximum profits. To increase engagement, algorithms have found that hate, misinformation, and politics are instrumental for app activity. The memo says: "The more incendiary the material, the more it keeps users engaged, the more it is boosted by the algorithm." A 2018 study found that "false rumors spread faster and wider than true information... They found falsehoods are 70% more likely to be retweeted on Twitter than the truth, and reach their first 1,500 people six times faster. This effect is more pronounced with political news than other categories."

### YouTube

YouTube has existed since 2005 and it has more than 2.5 billion monthly users. The YouTube discovery content systems are focused on the personal activity of the user (watched, favorites, likes) to direct them to recommended content. The algorithm of YouTube is responsible for roughly 70% of the videos recommended to users and it is what drives people to watch certain content. A 2022 study by the Mozilla Foundation found that users do not have much power to keep unsolicited videos out of the content that is recommended to them. This includes videos about hate speech, livestreams, etc.

- identified as influential platform for spreading radicalized content

  - result: extremism recommendations factor in radical keywords in video titles
- February 2023, Gonzalez v. Google: is Google (YouTube's parent) protected from lawsuits claiming algorithms aided terrorists by recommending ISIS videos
  - Section 230 generally protects platforms from civil liability for user content
- multiple studies: little to no evidence algorithms push far-right content to those not already engaged

- videos recommended to 'For You Page' (FYP); every user's page different
- FYP linked to more explicit and radical videos over time based on previous interactions
- since inception scrutinized for misinformation, hate speech -> generate more interactions
- 2022: head of US Security statement: [quote: 81,518,334 videos removed globally April – June] -> cut back hate speech, harassment, misinformation

steps.text:
### Facebook

The algorithm of Facebook is focused on recommending content that makes the user want to interact. It ranks content by giving priority to popular posts by friends, viral content, and sometimes divisive content. Every feed is personalized to the specific interests of the user, and this can sometimes lead users towards an echo chamber of troublesome content. Users can find the list of interests the algorithm uses by going to the "Your ad Preferences" page. A Pew Research study found that 74% of Facebook users did not know the list existed until the study directed them to that page. It is also fairly common for Facebook to assign political labels to its users. In recent years Facebook has started to use artificial intelligence to change the content that users see in their feed and what gets recommended to them. A document called The Facebook Files revealed that the AI system puts user engagement above everything else. The Facebook Files also showed that the AI systems have been difficult to control.

In an internal memo from August 2019 that was leaked in 2021, Facebook admitted that "the mechanics of our platforms are not neutral", and concluded that optimization for engagement is necessary to reach maximum profits. To increase engagement, algorithms have found that hate, misinformation, and politics are instrumental for app activity. The memo says: "The more incendiary the material, the more it keeps users engaged, the more it is boosted by the algorithm." A 2018 study found that "false rumors spread faster and wider than true information... They found falsehoods are 70% more likely to be retweeted on Twitter than the truth, and reach their first 1,500 people six times faster. This effect is more pronounced with political news than other categories."

### YouTube

YouTube has existed since 2005 and it has more than 2.5 billion monthly users. The YouTube discovery content systems are focused on the personal activity of the user (watched, favorites, likes) to direct them to recommended content. The algorithm of YouTube is responsible for roughly 70% of the videos recommended to users and it is what drives people to watch certain content. A 2022 study by the Mozilla Foundation found that users do not have much power to keep unsolicited videos out of the content that is recommended to them. This includes videos about hate speech, livestreams, etc.

YouTube has been identified as an influential platform for spreading radicalized content. Al-Qaeda and other extremist groups like it have been linked to using YouTube for recruitment videos and for engaging with international media outlets. A research study that was published by the American Behavioral Scientist Journal researched "whether it is possible to identify a set of attributes that may help explain part of the YouTube algorithm's decision-making process". The study's results showed that the presence of radical keywords in the title of a video factors into the YouTube algorithm's recommendations for extremism content. In February 2023, the case of Gonzalez v. Google asked whether Google, the parent company of YouTube, is protected from lawsuits that claim the site's algorithms aided terrorists by recommending ISIS videos to users. Section 230 is known to generally protect online platforms from civil liability for content their users post.

There are multiple studies that found little to no evidence that YouTube's algorithms direct attention towards far-right content for people who are not already engaged with it.

### TikTok

TikTok recommends videos to the 'For You Page' (FYP) of a user, so every user's page is different. Because of the nature of the algorithm behind the app, TikTok's FYP has been linked to showing more explicit and radical videos over time, based on the previous interactions of users on the app. Ever since TikTok started, the app has been scrutinized for misinformation and hate speech, since those kinds of media usually generate more interactions to the algorithm.

In 2022 the head of US Security at TikTok put out a statement that "81,518,334 videos were removed globally between April – June for violating our Community Guidelines or Terms of Service" in order to cut back on hate speech, harassment, and misinformation.

Studies have noted cases where individuals were radicalized through content they encountered on TikTok. For example, in early 2023 Austrian authorities thwarted a plot against an LGBTQ+ pride parade. The plot involved two teenagers and a 20-year-old who were inspired by jihadist content on TikTok. The youngest suspect was 14 years old and had been exposed to videos made by Islamist influencers that glorified jihad. These videos led him to engage more with similar content, and in the end he was involved in planning an attack.

In another case, in 2024 several teenagers were arrested in Vienna, Austria, who were planning to carry out a terrorist attack at a Taylor Swift concert. The investigation showed that some of the suspects had been radicalized online, and TikTok was one of the platforms used to spread extremist content that influenced their beliefs and actions.
